slides.title: Bollinger Bands Versus Your 1SD EMA Breakout
lines: A signal definition, not a claim of profitable trading.
A BAND TOUCH IS NOT A COMPLETE TRADE.
Distinguish a classic Bollinger Band from an EMA-centred volatility envelope.

slides.title: Should a band break be faded or followed?
lines: “Price touched the upper band. Isn’t it overbought?”
John Bollinger says a band tag alone is not a trade signal; trends can walk the bands.

slides.title: Original Bollinger versus your customised chart
lines: Common baseline: 20-period SMA, ±2 standard deviations of price.
Your SD lookback and centring method still need confirmation from the actual indicator script.

slides.title: An EMA-centred band needs two parameters
lines: n = mean period, m = standard-deviation sample; not necessarily the same.
Formula is a research hypothesis until actual TradingView code/settings are captured.

slides.title: Trend price can walk above a moving envelope
lines: Original instructional illustration — NOT observed price data.
Synthetic price and bands. A 1σ breach is more frequent than a wider 2σ breach, but frequency is not edge.

slides.title: Use words that can actually be backtested
lines: Wick touches the band; no close required.
Completed 4H candle closes beyond chosen upper/lower band.
Two or more completed closes beyond a defined threshold.
After the break, revisit the band under an exact tolerance rule.
The four patterns have different entry times and losses.

slides.title: The same technical event has two opposing interpretations
lines: Multiple band-side closes, rising/declining mean, aligned daily trend.
Low-trend regime, failed follow-through, close returns inside band.
These are competing hypotheses; neither wins automatically.

slides.title: 4H trigger and daily context do different jobs
lines: Identify dominant trend, last respected bands and major regime.
Define completed-bar break, hold/retest and entry timing.
100/200 EMA zones can be support/resistance hypotheses.
Cross-check real yields, DXY/JXY and upcoming catalysts.

slides.title: A falsifiable breakout example
lines: Same-close fills after a close-confirmed signal would create look-ahead bias.

slides.title: Your discretionary insight needs a rule
lines: A price-tested EMA envelope that previously held through retests.
Finite lookback, allowed wicks/closes, recency and what replaces the prior zone.
Without mechanical definitions, charts can be selected after seeing the winning outcome.

slides.title: A tighter band can make a worse trade
lines: ATR buffer + market structure → actual stop
No stop should be moved merely to fit an advertised prop percentage.
The band width is not the contract’s tick value or guaranteed maximum loss.

slides.title: Does 1σ help more than an ordinary breakout?
lines: Simple N-bar close breakout with identical exits.
Two closes and daily trend alignment.
Same dates, symbols, costs and risk treatment for a fair comparison.

slides.title: Evidence required before saying “it works”
lines: Exact SD formula, price source, 4H sessions and bar closes.
Untouched holdout and chronological walk-forward splits.
Bid/ask, slippage, tick economics and feasible tradable proxy.
Net expectancy, drawdown, tail losses, no-trades and regime stability.

slides.title: What a responsible preflight would ask
lines: Completed 4H close or only a wick?
Defined persistence or a hindsight retest?
Daily trend and event timing aligned?
Structure/ATR, tick value and actual risk?
A good setup description must permit a no-trade decision.

slides.title: What can and cannot be concluded?
lines: Does upper-band touch itself prove sell?
Are classic ±2σ SMA and EMA ±1σ the same?
Do more filters automatically increase true edge?
The real result requires an executable definition, pre-registered tests and a holdout.
